review_basis: Visually inspected all 23 original numbered Module 11 WebP slides directly, including the actual titles, diagrams, labels, examples and cautions; source order and concept boundaries were verified before narration.
part_title: Governance Policies, Ownership and Continuous Oversight

scenes.title: Importance of Governance and Compliance
scenes.narration: Read the four numbered governance stages across the slide. First, organizations define AI policies and assign oversight; IAM helps enforce access permissions, but permissions alone are not a policy. Second, they assess privacy and bias risks using appropriate testing and services such as SageMaker or Amazon Macie for sensitive-data discovery. Third, they retain evidence and review results; CloudWatch records useful monitoring signals while S3 can hold reports and evaluation artifacts. Fourth, accountable owners approve deployments and respond to problems. The loan example below illustrates why this matters: application data enters a model, governance checks assess fairness and sensitive information, and the result supports a transparent, reviewed decision. The monitoring panel closes the loop: check performance, unusual patterns and policy compliance, then take corrective action. Governance is an ongoing operating discipline, not a one-time checklist.

scenes.title: Governance Framework
scenes.narration: This picture has three linked pillars. Begin on the left with a cross-functional board: AI specialists contribute technical knowledge, legal staff cover obligations, privacy experts protect personal information, and compliance teams interpret policies. The middle pillar makes responsibility explicit. An owner is accountable, the decision-rights process defines who approves risky use cases or major changes, and escalation gives staff a way to raise concerns. The right pillar applies those decisions through the lifecycle: data sourcing and access, model training, deployment controls, and continuing monitoring. The service labels beneath are examples of implementation tools: S3 and Lake Formation support governed data, SageMaker and Bedrock support AI work, and CloudWatch or CloudTrail support operational evidence. In the enterprise assistant example, the board evaluates the use case and assigns approval authority before launch. Technical controls should support a human governance structure, not replace it.

scenes.title: Governance Tools: Choosing Evidence
scenes.narration: This is an exam comparison chart, not a pipeline. Across the top, associate each AWS tool with the question it answers. AWS Config records resource configurations and changes. Amazon Inspector identifies supported software vulnerabilities and unintended network exposure. AWS Audit Manager helps collect and organize audit evidence. AWS Artifact provides AWS compliance reports and selected agreements. AWS CloudTrail records API activity, such as who called an operation and when. Trusted Advisor checks an AWS environment against supported best-practice recommendations. Follow the six questions in the middle row and match the evidence type instead of choosing a tool because its name sounds security-related. For instance, if an auditor requests who changed a resource, investigate CloudTrail activity; if they want configuration history, use Config. A company may need several kinds of evidence for the same audit. None of these services independently guarantees regulatory compliance.

scenes.title: Governance Strategies
scenes.narration: Follow the five large steps and especially the decision diamond. Step one defines policies for data privacy, model development and acceptable outputs. Step two implements technical checks; the pictured examples are protected data in S3, model evaluation in SageMaker and safeguards in Bedrock. Step three combines technical assessment with human legal and policy review. At the diamond, approve only when policy, legal and technical requirements are met. A failed check goes to rework, then returns for validation; it must not be quietly bypassed. Step five establishes a recurring review schedule because new data, models and threats can change risk. The financial-services example uses S3 data controls, SageMaker bias and performance checks, Bedrock output safeguards and staff approval. This is continuous governance: technical checks produce evidence, people make decisions, and monitoring can reopen the review.

scenes.title: Transparency, Accountability and Training
scenes.narration: The four colored panels form a repeating responsible-AI cycle. First, publish what the model can do, what it cannot do and the situations where it should be used. Second, let users and affected people report incorrect or harmful results. Third, name a person or team responsible for investigating and fixing issues, rather than leaving ownership vague. Fourth, train the support and development teams on fairness, limitations and proper use. Follow the lower customer-support example: a model card and user guidance explain limits, customer or agent feedback identifies problems, an accountable owner tracks resolution, and staff training prevents repeated mistakes. The return arrows show why this never ends. For the multiple-select exam question, all four depicted actions support responsible AI. Documentation without feedback, or feedback without accountable follow-through, is incomplete governance.
